titulo: Where the simulator lies about a humanoid
lead: A policy that walks in the simulator and falls on the robot: that is the problem of this course. In this lesson you set up the bench, run the ready-made Unitree G1 gait policy in the "sim" and in a "simulated real" with hidden parameters, and find out that no single difference knocks it down; the sum of them does.
objetivo: measure the gap by running the same policy in "sim" and "simulated real", and find that no single parameter brings it down.

aprende.t: The five sources of the gap in a humanoid: actuator, latency, friction, mass, and contact
The ready-made G1 gait policy (unitree_rl_lab) running in MuJoCo
Sim × "simulated real": 4.7 m walked versus a fall in 2.3 s
Change one parameter at a time to find the culprit

hero_alt: Humanoid robot mid-step on a smooth lab floor, with the foot slipping and a safety cable attached to the gantry.

secoes.sub: Click each block. These are the five sources of gap this course measures.

nos.detalhe: In the simulator, the motor delivers exactly the PD torque: kp × error − kd × velocity. On the robot, the transmission, heating, and firmware change the effective gain and the maximum torque. Lesson 3 (identify) and lesson 4 (limit).
The policy decides at 50 Hz; the command travels over the network, and the motor's PD runs at 500 Hz–1 kHz. Every millisecond between the state read and the torque applied counts. Lesson 4.
The friction coefficient between the foot and the floor changes with the surface, the sole, and dust. Below a certain value, the foot slips on stance. Lesson 2.
Swapped battery, an extra camera, a cable: the real mass and center of mass differ from the file. Lesson 2.
Foot-ground contact is the most simplified part of any physics engine: stiffness, damping, and sliding are approximations. That is why you validate in more than one engine (lesson 6).

secoes.legenda: None of these differences go away. Sim-to-real means making the policy robust to them, measuring the ones you can measure, and testing before the floor.

secoes.titulo: The policy and the two worlds
secoes.sub: What runs in this course's practice sessions. Click each step.

texto: Unitree publishes in unitree_rl_lab a G1 29-DoF walking policy already trained in Isaac Lab and exported to ONNX, with the deployment file deploy.yaml (joint order, kp and kd, default pose, scales). Apache-2.0 license.
It takes 480 numbers (5 timesteps of angular velocity, projected gravity, command, joints, and last action) and returns 29 position targets at 50 Hz.
The MuJoCo Menagerie G1 (the same one from course 0) with the policy's PD inside MuJoCo: a position actuator with the kp and kd from deploy.yaml.
Running a policy trained in Isaac Lab inside MuJoCo already means crossing from one physics engine to another.

You don't have a G1. The course's "real robot" is the same MuJoCo with four hidden parameters in kit/mundos/real.json. Don't open the file before lesson 3: there you discover one of them through system identification.
It's a bench test, not the robot: what it teaches is the method, not the number.
--so kp makes the "real" differ only in kp. Running each parameter alone, you see that none of them knocks the policy down, but kp alone already makes it walk 50% faster than commanded.
The gap is rarely a single cause: it's the sum of small differences.

secoes.titulo: Set up the bench (reuses the one from course 0)
secoes.sub: If you did course 0, the venv and the Menagerie are already in ~/fth: this block only adds onnxruntime, the G1 in the sparse-checkout, and the unitree_rl_lab policy folder, pinned to the tested commit.

blocos.conteudo:
F=${FTH:-$HOME/fth}; mkdir -p $F && cd $F
[ -d .venv ] || python3.12 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate && pip install -q mujoco==3.16.0 numpy onnxruntime==1.31.0 pyyaml
[ -d sim2real ] || git clone -q --depth 1 https://github.com/inematds/formacao-fth-sim2real-v72 sim2real
[ -d mujoco_menagerie ] || git clone -q --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/google-deepmind/mujoco_menagerie
git -C mujoco_menagerie sparse-checkout add unitree_g1 && git -C mujoco_menagerie checkout -q 62ab00f
[ -d unitree_rl_lab ] || git clone -q --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/unitreerobotics/unitree_rl_lab
git -C unitree_rl_lab sparse-checkout set deploy/robots/g1_29dof/config/policy/velocity
git -C unitree_rl_lab checkout -q 4960b84 && git -C unitree_rl_lab log -1 --format='unitree_rl_lab %h (%ad)' --date=short
python3 -c "import mujoco, onnxruntime; print('mujoco', mujoco.__version__, '· onnxruntime', onnxruntime.__version__)"

secoes.titulo: The same policy in both worlds
secoes.sub: dois_mundos.py runs 10 s walking at 0.5 m/s in each world. Fall = pelvis below 0.5 m. Exits with 1 if any world fell.

blocos.rot: Terminal · one parameter at a time
blocos.conteudo:
F=${FTH:-$HOME/fth}; cd $F/sim2real && . $F/.venv/bin/activate
for p in atrito massa kp atraso_ms; do python3 kit/dois_mundos.py --so $p | tail -1; done

política: unitree_rl_lab G1 29 GDL velocity v0 (ONNX, 480 entradas) · comando 0.50 m/s · 10 s
sim                          queda: não · andou 4.7 m em 10 s (vel. 0.47 m/s; pedida 0.50)
real simulado                queda: sim em t = 2.3 s (andou 1.9 m)
saída: 1

In the sim, 4.7 m in 10 s (0.47 m/s for 0.50 commanded). In the "simulated real," a fall at 2.3 s.

real simulado (só atrito)    queda: não · andou 4.7 m em 10 s (vel. 0.47 m/s; pedida 0.50)
real simulado (só massa)     queda: não · andou 4.6 m em 10 s (vel. 0.46 m/s; pedida 0.50)
real simulado (só kp)        queda: não · andou 7.5 m em 10 s (vel. 0.75 m/s; pedida 0.50)
real simulado (só atraso_ms) queda: não · andou 4.6 m em 10 s (vel. 0.46 m/s; pedida 0.50)

None alone knocks it down. kp alone makes the robot walk at 0.75 m/s: the softer PD lets the legs lag behind, and the policy compensates by pushing harder.

secoes.sub: The explanation appears after your answer.

perguntas.p: Each parameter of the "simulated real" robot, on its own, does not knock the policy down; all four together do. What does this teach?
opcoes: That the gap is usually the sum of several small differences.
That the simulator got the fall calculation wrong in the real world.
That the policy only works with kp exactly equal to the one in the file.
That friction is always the main cause of a fall.
perguntas.explica: Each difference takes away a little margin. Together, they go past what the policy can handle. That's why you measure one at a time and then test the combination.

perguntas.p: Running a policy trained in Isaac Lab on MuJoCo is already:
opcoes: An error, because the policy only works in the training simulator.
Training the policy again, now on MuJoCo.
A sim2sim: crossing from one physics engine to another.
The same as running on the robot, because both use the same URDF.
perguntas.explica: Different engines approximate contact and the actuator in different ways. Walking in both is a first sign of robustness; it's the gate of lesson 6.

perguntas.p: With only the lower kp, the robot walks at 0.75 m/s when the request is 0.50. Why?
opcoes: The lower kp raises the maximum torque of each motor.
The softer PD delays the legs and the policy compensates by pushing harder.
The velocity command is multiplied by kp before it reaches the policy.
MuJoCo reduces foot friction when kp decreases.
perguntas.explica: The policy is a closed loop: if the joints don't reach the target, it asks for more. The result is walking wrong without falling, a gap that only shows up when you measure the speed.

itens.texto: Actuator, latency (delay), friction, mass, and contact set the simulator apart from the robot.
The same policy walks 4.7 m in sim and falls at 2.3 s in the "simulated real" robot.
One parameter at a time finds the culprit; it's the sum that knocks it down.
